story_contract.opening_question: In Texas, when documentation is AI-generated, who verifies the output?
story_contract.actor: UT Physicians, Abridge, University of Texas REAL Health AI and the Texas Act that took effect September 1st, 2025.
story_contract.action: UT Physicians is working toward Epic's ambient listening platform, Abridge announced an agreement with University of Texas REAL Health AI and the Texas Act conditions AI diagnostic use on review of AI records.
story_contract.change: Visit notes at UT health institutions can be drafted by AI from the conversation for a clinician to verify.
story_contract.affected_people: Physicians who review the drafts and the patients whose visits are the source. No person is named or drawn.
story_contract.consequence: A clinician is expected to review a draft note that software wrote from the visit.
story_contract.source_limit: The Abridge claims are the vendor's own. The school page gives no date, accuracy or time figure. The bill is written around diagnosis and doesn't say whether a visit note counts.
story_contract.closing_answer: The vendor's design and the statute's review condition both point the check at the clinician, and none of these sources says how well that check works.

captions.text: In Texas, when documentation is AI-generated,
who verifies the output?
UT Physicians is working toward adopting a unified system,
Epic's ambient listening platform.
It follows pilot programs involving DAX and Abridge.
The technology would eventually be available to physicians,
with an Epic refresher.
On October 8th, 2026,
Abridge announced an enterprise-wide agreement,
with University of Texas REAL Health AI.
Abridge says UT health institutions can access Abridge,
preserving local decision-making.
Linked Evidence, Abridge says,
maps documentation to source data.
Clinicians can then verify the output.
A Texas Act took effect September 1st, 2025.
It covers artificial intelligence used for diagnostic purposes.
Its conditions include review of all AI-created records,
under Texas Medical Board standards.
That law is written around diagnosis.
The bill doesn't say whether a visit note counts.
Abridge says clinicians can verify.
The law requires review for diagnostic use.
No source here says how well that check works.
